# Kaoken (baked-weight C code generation for CPU transformer inference)

<sub>[fastpp](../../../README.md) › [Catalog](../../README.md) › [Numerics and science](../README.md) › [Autodiff and ML kernels](README.md)</sub>

**Tier C** (first-party claim) · Copyable · `C (generated by a Python tool)` · `MIT` · 🟡 stale

> Python generator that emits GPT-2 layers as straight-line C with baked weights; first-party per-layer timings beat PyTorch CPU.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Beats** | PyTorch CPU layers (transformers GPT-2 building blocks) |
| **Claimed result** | PyTorch vs Kaoken in ms: LayerNorm 0.052 vs 0.0052; GELU 0.174 vs 0.084; Linear 22.4 vs 2.378; Attention 14.484 vs 9.386 (about 10x, 2.1x, 9.4x and 1.5x, derived from page data). |
| **Workload** | Per-layer CPU timings of GPT-2 blocks at batch 1 (LayerNorm [1,768], GELU [1,768], Linear [768,50257], Attention [1,768]), average of five runs, no GPU. |
| **Metric** | latency |
| **Compiler and flags** | clang -arch arm64 -O3 (generated/Makefile; NEON intrinsics in the generated code). The README does not say which build or machine produced the benchmark numbers. |
| **Adoption** | 4 stars |
| **Last commit** | 2024-11-16 |
| **Links** | [repository](https://github.com/sushrut141/kaoken) · [benchmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sushrut141/kaoken/HEAD/README.md) |

## Verdict

The README table times single PyTorch layer calls (time.time(), no warm-up) against single generated-C calls (clock()), averaged over five runs, on an unstated ARM64 machine (MacBook Air implied) with torch 2.0.1 pinned: LayerNorm [1,768] 0.052 vs 0.0052 ms, GELU 0.174 vs 0.084 ms, Linear [768,50257] 22.4 vs 2.378 ms, Attention 14.484 vs 9.386 ms, all with synthetic patterned weights rather than GPT-2's. The margin likely comes mostly from PyTorch cold-call overhead and constant folding over repeated weights.

## Use it when

- Studying how far constant-folding and full unrolling of a tiny, fixed-shape layer can go on an ARM64 (Apple Silicon) CPU with clang -O3.
- Prototyping a code-generation backend for a very small model whose weights fit comfortably in generated source.
- As a teaching example of turning a PyTorch module into specialized C, with the PyTorch validation scripts as reference outputs.

## Skip it when

- Real GPT-2 or any real model inference: the README says baked attention with actual GPT-2 weights (16k lines of C) could not be compiled on a MacBook Air, and no end-to-end model.generate() benchmark exists.
- x86-64 or any non-ARM target: the templates include arm_neon.h and the Makefile hard-codes clang -arch arm64.
- Large layers such as the lm_head Linear [768 x 50257]: fully unrolled, that is about 38.6 million literal multiply-adds in one function, so compile time, memory and code size are prohibitive.
- Models whose weights change or need quantization; every weight change means regenerating and recompiling the C.
- Anything that needs a maintained project: 17 commits over about one month in late 2024, no releases, no tests beyond the validation scripts.

## How it is fast

Ahead-of-time specialization: shapes and weights are known at generation time, so the generator (utils.unroll_loops plus MAT_MULTIPLY / MAT_MULTIPLY_TRANSPOSE macros) explodes every matrix multiply into one multiply-add expression per output element with constant weights, removing loops, framework dispatch and tensor allocation. LayerNorm uses hand-written ARM NEON intrinsics (vld1q_f32, vaddvq_f32, vdivq_f32). The measured gap also includes PyTorch's per-call Python and dispatch overhead, which dominates at batch 1 and [1,768].

## Compared with alternatives

Pick Kaoken only to study baked-weight code generation on ARM; CodeJeNN is the closer working 'emit C++ from a trained model' tool, llm.c's train_gpt2.c is a readable, working plain-C GPT-2, and CTranslate2 or OpenVINO are what to deploy for real CPU transformer inference.

## Integration

| | |
|---|---|
| **Form** | source-drop (generated .c files) |
| **Dependencies** | Generation: Python with torch 2.0.1, transformers 4.34.1, numpy 1.26.1 (requirements.txt) and a local GPT-2 checkout; generated code: libc and libm only |
| **Minimum toolchain** | clang with ARM NEON support (Makefile: clang -arch arm64 -O3); C standard not documented |
| **Platforms** | aarch64 only (arm_neon.h, -arch arm64); Apple Silicon implied by the Makefile and the README's MacBook Air mention |
| **Thread safety** | not documented; generated attention code keeps intermediate results in global heap buffers (gpt2_attention_0_c_attn_temp etc.), so concurrent calls into the same layer would race |
| **Drop-in for the baseline** | no |

## Gotchas

- The committed generated/\*.c files are toy shapes (10x10 Linear, 4-element LayerNorm, embedding size 8 attention), not the [1,768] and [768,50257] shapes in the benchmark table; the code that produced the table is not in the repo.
- The validation Linear weights repeat the same row for every output feature (every row is 0.1\*(i+1)), and the committed 10x10 test bakes 0.1 everywhere, so after unrolling every output is the same expression and clang -O3 can fold them into a single dot product; the 22.4 ms vs 2.378 ms Linear ratio may not reflect real lm_head work.
- Weights are baked as double literals (e.g. input[0][1] \* 0.1) and GELU calls pow/tanh/sqrt in double with pi approximated as 3.14159, so results drift slightly from PyTorch's float32 math.pi version.
- Generated code mallocs its buffers and never frees them, and attention needs gpt2_attention_0_initialize_heap_memory() called first.

## Known shortcomings

- PyTorch is timed as one cold first call with no warm-up (validation/\*.py) while the C side uses clock(); weights are synthetic patterned values, not GPT-2. Ratios are likely overstated.
- Claim not reproducible: committed generated/\*.c are toy shapes (10x10 Linear, 4-element LayerNorm), not the benchmarked [768,50257] code, which is not in the repo. Validation Linear weights repeat the same row for every output, so after unrolling clang -O3 can fold every output into one dot product; the 9.4x Linear ratio likely does not reflect real work. ARM64 only; nothing works end to end.

## Caveats and trade-offs

CPU model, PyTorch version and thread count are not stated (generated/Makefile targets arm64 with clang -O3 and the README mentions a MacBook Air, so Apple Silicon is implied but not stated). Methodology is weak: validation/linear.py and validation/layer_normalization.py time a single cold first call of the PyTorch layer with time.time() (no warm-up), the generated C main() times one call with clock(), and 'average of five runs' means five such runs, so PyTorch's first-call overhead likely inflates the gap, especially for LayerNorm and GELU at [1,768]. The weights are synthetic patterns from the validation scripts (e.g. every Linear row is 0.1\*(i+1)), not GPT-2 weights, and they are baked into the C source as constants. The README says baked layers with real GPT-2 weights could not be compiled on a MacBook Air, the MLP row has no Kaoken number, end-to-end model.generate() benchmarks were never done, and the headline still reads 'by X%'. About one month of commit history (Oct-Nov 2024, 17 commits); first-party.

Weights are baked into generated source and matmuls are unrolled into straight-line code, so each model needs its own generated, very large C file; only GPT-2 layers implemented; CPU only; Python tooling required to generate.

## Maintenance

Stale prototype (last commit 2024-11-16, 17 commits, 4 stars), MIT-licensed so code is copyable, but nothing works end to end and it needs regeneration per model.
